entries.title: What a budget actually does
entries.text: A budget is not a restriction, it is a record of decisions you have already made. Writing down where money goes turns vague worry into a number you can argue with. Most people who start tracking find one or two categories are far larger than they guessed.

entries.title: The 50/30/20 split
entries.text: A common starting shape: about 50% of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for saving and debt repayment. Treat it as a first draft rather than a rule. High rent or a low income shifts the split, and that is fine as long as it is deliberate.

entries.title: Pay yourself first
entries.text: Move money to savings on the day you are paid, not from whatever survives the month. Anything left at the end tends to be nothing, because spending expands to fill the balance in the account.

entries.title: The emergency fund
entries.text: Three to six months of essential expenses, kept somewhere boring and reachable within a day. Its job is to absorb a lost job, a hospital bill or a broken phone without borrowing. It is not an investment and should not be invested.

entries.title: Debt that buys something, and debt that does not
entries.text: Borrowing for a house or an education buys an asset or an income. Borrowing for a holiday or a gadget buys the thing plus the interest. The label matters less than the rate: any debt above roughly 10% a year is worth clearing before investing.

entries.title: Compound interest, working for you
entries.text: Interest earns interest. At 8% a year money roughly doubles in nine years, so the same amount saved at 25 is worth far more at 60 than money saved at 40. Starting early matters more than picking the right moment.

entries.title: Compound interest, working against you
entries.text: The same maths runs in reverse on a credit card. Paying only the minimum on a balance at 3% a month can take years and cost more in interest than the original purchase. Clear the highest rate first.

entries.title: Track before you cut
entries.text: Spend one month recording everything without changing anything. Cutting before you have data usually removes small pleasures while leaving the large leaks untouched.

entries.title: Sinking funds
entries.text: For costs that are certain but not monthly, such as tuition, insurance or a yearly trip, divide the amount by twelve and set it aside each month. This turns a shock into a line item.

entries.title: Lifestyle creep
entries.text: When income rises, spending quietly rises to match and the saving rate stays flat. The fix is to decide in advance what share of any raise gets saved, before the money arrives.

entries.title: Insurance is for what you cannot absorb
entries.text: Insure the events that would ruin you: serious illness, losing the earner, the house burning down. Do not insure what you could pay for out of savings. Extended warranties on small electronics are usually a poor trade.

entries.title: Investing, briefly
entries.text: Broad, low-cost index funds held for decades beat most attempts at picking individual stocks, mostly because fees and trading compound against you. Anything promising a high return with no risk is not telling the truth.
